title: Chapter 93 — The Castaway
paragraphs: It was only some few days after encountering the Frenchman that a most significant event befell the most insignificant of the Pequod's crew — an event most lamentable, and which ended in providing the sometimes madly merry and predestined craft with a living and ever-accompanying prophecy of whatever shattered fate might prove her own.

Now, on a whale-ship, not everyone goes in the boats. Some few hands are held back as ship-keepers, whose job it is to work the vessel while the boats are chasing the whale. As a general thing, these ship-keepers are as hardy as the men in the boats' crews. But if there happens to be an unduly slender, clumsy, or timid fellow on the ship, that fellow is certain to be made a ship-keeper. It was so on the Pequod with the little negro Pippin — Pip, for short. Poor Pip! You have heard of him before. You must remember his tambourine on that dramatic midnight, so gloomy-jolly.

In outward appearance, Pip and Dough-Boy made a matched pair, like a black pony and a white one of equal size though different color, driven in one wild harness. But while hapless Dough-Boy was by nature dull and sluggish in his wits, Pip, though over tender-hearted, was at bottom very bright, with that pleasant, warm, jolly brightness peculiar to his people — a people who ever enjoy all holidays and festivities with finer, freer relish than any other race. For blacks, the year's calendar should show nothing but three hundred and sixty-five Fourth of Julys and New Year's Days. Nor smile while I write that this little black boy was brilliant, for even blackness has its brilliance: behold that lustrous ebony, paneled in kings' cabinets. But Pip loved life and all life's peaceful securities, so that the panic-striking business in which he had somehow become entangled had most sadly dimmed his brightness — though, as will soon be seen, what was thus temporarily subdued in him was destined in the end to be luridly illuminated by strange wild fires, that falsely showed him off to ten times the natural luster with which, in his native Tolland County in Connecticut, he had once enlivened many a fiddler's dance on the green and, at melodious twilight, with his gay laughter had turned the round horizon into one star-belled tambourine. So, though in the clear light of day a pure diamond drop suspended against a blue-veined neck will glow with healthy beauty, yet when the cunning jeweler would show you the diamond in its most impressive luster, he lays it against a gloomy background and then lights it up not by the sun but by some unnatural gas. Then come those fiery blazes, infernally superb. Then the evil-blazing diamond, once the divinest symbol of the crystal skies, looks like some crown-jewel stolen from the King of Hell. But let us get to the story.
It came to pass that in the ambergris affair, Stubb's rear oarsman happened to sprain his hand so badly as to be temporarily disabled. And so Pip was put in his place.

The first time Stubb lowered with him, Pip showed much nervousness. But happily, that time he escaped close contact with the whale, and therefore came off not altogether badly — though Stubb, observing him, afterward took care to urge him to nurture his courage to the utmost, for he might often find it necessary.

Now upon the second lowering, the boat paddled up to the whale. As the fish received the darted harpoon, it gave its customary jolt, which happened in this instance to be right under poor Pip's seat. The involuntary shock of the moment caused him to leap, paddle in hand, out of the boat. And in such a way that part of the slack whale-line, coming against his chest, he carried it overboard with him, becoming entangled in it when he plunged into the water. That instant the struck whale started on a fierce run. The line swiftly straightened, and — presto! — poor Pip came foaming up to the bow of the boat, remorselessly dragged there by the line, which had taken several turns around his chest and neck.

Tashtego stood in the bow. He was full of the fire of the hunt. He despised Pip for a coward. Snatching the boat-knife from its sheath, he held its sharp edge over the line, and turning toward Stubb, cried: "Cut?" Meanwhile, Pip's blue, choking face plainly pleaded: Do, for God's sake! All passed in a flash. In less than half a minute, the whole thing happened.
"Damn him, cut!" roared Stubb. And so the whale was lost and Pip was saved.

As soon as he recovered himself, the poor little negro was assailed by yells and curses from the crew. Calmly letting these irregular damnations blow over, Stubb then in a plain, businesslike, but still half-humorous manner, cursed Pip officially. And that done, unofficially gave him much wholesome advice. The substance was: Never jump from a boat, Pip, except — but all the rest was indefinite, as the soundest advice ever is. Now, in general, "Stick to the boat" is the true motto in whaling. But cases will sometimes arise when "Leap from the boat" is still better. Moreover, as if realizing at last that if he gave Pip fully conscientious advice, he would be leaving him too wide a margin to jump in for the future, Stubb suddenly dropped all counsel and concluded with a flat command: "Stick to the boat, Pip, or by the Lord, I won't pick you up if you jump. Mind that. We can't afford to lose whales because of the likes of you. A whale would sell for thirty times what you would, Pip, in Alabama. Bear that in mind, and don't jump anymore." Hereby perhaps Stubb indirectly hinted that though man loved his fellow, yet man is a money-making animal, a tendency that too often interferes with his kindness.

But we are all in the hands of the Gods, and Pip jumped again. It was under very similar circumstances to the first time, but now he did not carry the line overboard with him. And so when the whale started to run, Pip was left behind on the sea, like a hurried traveler's forgotten trunk. Alas! Stubb was but too true to his word. It was a beautiful, bountiful, blue day. The spangled sea was calm and cool, stretching flatly away on all sides to the horizon, like gold-beater's skin hammered out to the extreme. Bobbing up and down in that sea, Pip's dark head showed like a head of cloves. No boat-knife was lifted when he fell so rapidly astern. Stubb's inexorable back was turned upon him, and the whale was struck. In three minutes, a whole mile of shoreless ocean lay between Pip and Stubb. Out from the center of the sea, poor Pip turned his crisp, curling, black head to the sun — another lonely castaway, though the loftiest and the brightest.

Now in calm weather, to swim in the open ocean is as easy for the practiced swimmer as to ride in a carriage on shore. But the awful loneliness is intolerable. The intense concentration of self in the middle of such a heartless immensity — my God! Who can tell it? Notice how when sailors in a dead calm bathe in the open sea, they hug their ship and only swim along her sides.

But had Stubb really abandoned the poor little negro to his fate? No — he did not mean to, at least. Because there were two boats in his wake, and he supposed, no doubt, that they would quickly come up to Pip and pick him up. Though, indeed, such consideration toward oarsmen endangered through their own timidity is not always shown by the hunters in similar cases. And such cases occur not infrequently. Almost invariably in the fishery, a coward, so called, is marked with the same ruthless contempt peculiar to military navies and armies.

But it so happened that those boats, without seeing Pip, suddenly spotted whales close to them on one side, turned, and gave chase. And Stubb's boat was now so far away, and he and all his crew so intent upon their whale, that Pip's ringed horizon began to expand around him miserably. By the merest chance, the ship itself at last rescued him. But from that hour the little negro went about the deck an idiot — such, at least, they said he was. The sea had mockingly kept his finite body up but drowned the infinite of his soul. Not drowned entirely, though. Rather carried down alive to wondrous depths, where strange shapes of the unwarped primal world glided to and fro before his passive eyes. And the miser-merman, Wisdom, revealed his hoarded heaps. And among the joyous, heartless, ever-youthful eternities, Pip saw the multitudinous, God-omnipresent coral insects that out of the firmament of waters heaved the colossal orbs. He saw God's foot upon the treadle of the loom, and spoke it. And therefore his shipmates called him mad. So man's insanity is heaven's sense. And wandering from all mortal reason, man comes at last to that celestial thought which, to reason, is absurd and frantic — and, weal or woe, feels then uncompromised, indifferent as his God.
For the rest, do not blame Stubb too harshly. The thing is common in that fishery. And in the sequel of the narrative, it will be seen what like abandonment befell myself.
